analysis.one_liner: Repeals the requirement that federal construction contractors pay workers the locally prevailing wage.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote, so the Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage requirement for federal construction workers remained in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors on federally funded construction — buildings, roads, and other public works — to pay workers the wage that prevails locally for their trade. This bill would have wiped out that requirement and voided every reference to it in other laws, effective 30 days after enactment, while leaving existing contracts alone. It never advanced: after introduction it was sent to the Senate labor committee and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the bill would have benefited federal construction contractors who want to bid using lower-paid labor, by freeing them from the requirement to pay locally prevailing wages on government projects. Supporters argued it would also lower construction costs for taxpayers on federal projects.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's only stated mechanism was cost reduction for the federal government and contractors: it repealed the requirement that locally prevailing wages be paid on federally financed construction.

It voided all references in other laws to the Davis-Bacon wage requirements, removing the wage floor not just from direct federal contracts but from federally assisted construction across other programs.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federal projects would have borne the cost, since their pay would be set by contractors rather than by the local prevailing-wage standard; many would likely have seen lower wages and benefits on federally funded jobs.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Davis-Bacon would lower the labor-cost floor on federal construction, which supporters argued would reduce what the government pays for building projects.
Supporters of repeal argued prevailing-wage rules add paperwork and compliance costs to federal contracts and that market wages should govern.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had no offsetting benefit for workers; its stated aim was to lower labor costs on federal projects by removing the prevailing-wage floor. Because it never received a vote or a hearing, workers on federal construction kept the existing wage protections, and the public avoided the risk of lower-quality, lower-wage federal construction.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved; no hearing, no vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Lee introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act in the Senate on March 17, 2021, with 12 Republican cosponsors.
The Senate's only action was to read the bill twice and refer it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee; no further action was taken for the rest of the 117th Congress.

Had it passed, the bill would have repealed the Davis-Bacon Act's requirement that contractors on federally financed construction pay the locally prevailing wage, and voided all references to that requirement in other laws.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federal projects came out ahead, since the prevailing-wage requirement that sets a wage floor on their jobs survived; contractors who want to pay less than prevailing wages lost the repeal they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers, whose prevailing-wage floor survived

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage requirement.

for.name: Senate HELP Committee (Chair Patty Murray, D-WA)
for.what_they_did: Received the referral and never took the bill up; no hearing or markup occurred, ending the bill's prospects.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats supported it, and the Democratic-controlled Senate committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Unionized and prevailing-wage construction contractors and workers
industries.note: The bill would have removed the Davis-Bacon wage floor that covers them on federal projects; its failure left the standard in place. Keeping the standard preserves a wage baseline that limits a low-wage race to the bottom on public construction.

industries.industry: Non-union and low-wage federal construction contractors
industries.note: Repeal would have let these firms bid on federal work paying below-local wages and cut labor costs; it failed, so that opening did not happen.
